title: Spider Crater: The mysterious mark left by an ancient meteorite
excerpt: NASA satellite imagery reveals Spider Crater in Western Australia, where an ancient meteorite impact left a remarkable spider-shaped formation.
content:
NASA satellite imagery reveals Spider Crater in Western Australia, where an ancient meteorite impact left a remarkable spider-shaped formation.

Today’s Image of the Day from NASA Earth Observatory reveals a strange formation in Western Australia that looks remarkably like a giant spider stretching across the landscape. 

The name of the formation, Spider Crater, could hardly be more fitting.

But this enormous spider is not alive. It is the battered remains of a meteorite impact that occurred hundreds of millions of years ago.

Located in the remote Kimberley region, Spider Crater offers a remarkable glimpse into Earth’s ancient geological history. 

NASA’s Landsat 9 satellite captured this unusual landscape on September 20, 2026, using its Operational Land Imager (OLI).

A giant spider carved into the landscape

The full impact structure measures approximately 8 miles long and 7 miles wide.

At its center lies the most recognizable feature: a spider-shaped formation spanning roughly 2.5 miles.

The pale ridges forming the spider’s legs consist of sandstone that has resisted erosion better than the surrounding rock.

Over millions of years, wind, water, and weathering gradually stripped away softer layers, leaving behind the dramatic pattern visible from space today.

Interestingly, the spider shape is not the original outline of the meteorite crater. 

Scientists believe it represents a central uplift, a mound of rock that rose from the crater floor after the impact.

When a large asteroid or other space rock strikes Earth, the immense force compresses the ground. 

The underlying rock then rebounds upward, somewhat like the surface of water after something heavy falls into it.

At Spider Crater, that rebound helped create the structure that erosion would eventually expose.

How scientists solved the crater mystery

Spider Crater’s unusual appearance initially puzzled geologists.

For decades after its discovery, researchers debated how the formation had developed. Some suspected volcanic activity rather than a meteorite impact.

The decisive evidence came from rocks within the crater itself.

Geologists discovered distinctive fractures known as shatter cones, which form when extremely powerful shock waves pass through rock.

These fractures are among the clearest geological signs of a meteorite impact.

At Spider Crater, shatter cones occur throughout the central dome, providing strong evidence that an extraterrestrial object struck the region long ago.

Researchers have also examined microscopic changes in quartz and zircon crystals recovered from the sandstone.

These minerals preserve evidence of the intense pressures generated during an impact. Their altered structures can help scientists investigate the direction and conditions of the ancient collision.

A visitor from Earth’s distant past

Although scientists have established Spider Crater’s impact origin, its precise age remains uncertain.

Based on the surrounding geological formations, researchers estimate that the space rock struck between 600 million and 900 million years ago.

That places the collision in the late Precambrian, an extraordinary chapter of Earth’s history.

During this vast interval, life existed primarily in the oceans, and complex animal ecosystems had not yet emerged in the form familiar today.

The continents also looked very different from those we recognize on modern maps.

Since the impact, hundreds of millions of years of geological change have erased much of the crater’s original appearance.

What remains is an intricate network of sandstone ridges, preserved in one of Australia’s most remote landscapes.

Why ancient impact craters are so difficult to find

Earth has been struck by countless asteroids and meteorites throughout its history, but relatively few ancient impact craters remain recognizable today.

Unlike the Moon, where impact scars can survive for billions of years, Earth constantly reshapes its surface. 

Erosion wears down mountains and craters, while tectonic activity can bury or destroy evidence of ancient collisions.

Spider Crater illustrates how dramatically an impact site can change over time. 

Its original impact depression has largely disappeared, leaving behind only fragments of the geological structures created by the collision.

Without the distinctive shatter cones preserved in its rocks, scientists might never have recognized its extraterrestrial origins.

Spider Crater is a reminder that Earth’s surface holds traces of violent events from its distant past. 

Sometimes, those traces take on shapes that are as surprising as the events that created them.
